links.comparator_used: AI-standalone (AI outputs every prediction without radiologist consultation); also radiologist alone
links.outcome: False negatives and false positives for fracture detection, and their clinical consequences
links.effect: AI-triage (radiologist consulted when AI in doubt): 2.1% FN (32/1508; 18 consequences), 1.7% FP (26/1508). AI-standalone: 1.5% FN (23/1508; 11 consequences), 6.8% FP (103/1508). Radiologist alone: 2.7% FN, 1.2% FP.
links.tradeoff: Triage had more missed fractures and more with clinical consequences than standalone AI. It increased FN in all experience subgroups except radiologists-in-training. It did reduce FP compared with standalone AI.
links.quote: These results suggest AI should not be considered for problem-solving or triage at this time; AI standalone performs better than either and may be a source of assistance where radiologists are unavailable.

links.comparator_used: Radiologist diagnosis alone and AI-standalone (AI acting alone)
links.outcome: Missed fractures (FN) with clinical consequences, and false positives, using AI as a safety net when the radiologist diagnosis is negative
links.effect: AI-safety net: 0.07% FN (1/1508; 1 consequence), 7.6% FP (115/1508). Radiologist alone: 2.7% FN (40/1508; 28 consequences), 1.2% FP. AI-standalone: 1.5% FN (23/1508; 11 consequences), 6.8% FP.
links.tradeoff: False positives rose from 1.2% to 7.6%, although the authors say unnecessary treatments remain limited.
links.quote: Best results were obtained implementing AI as safety net, which eliminates missed fractures with serious clinical consequences; even though false positives are increased, unnecessary treatments are limited.

design_hint: workflow integration modes (standalone vs problem-solving vs triage vs safety-net)
